rejected.title: Satire and parody
card: Satire
a text that uses humour, irony and exaggeration to criticise people, habits or ideas. Its aim is to make the reader see a fault and think about it.
Parody
a text that copies the style of another text, such as its layout, voice or format, to mock it or to make a point. The reader must know the original to see the joke.

Example: a news article reports that the town council has banned Tuesdays to save money. The calm news voice and the silly claim make fun of wasteful decisions. This is satire, and it is also a parody of a news report.
Satire is about what it criticises. Parody is about how it copies. A text can do both, but a parody does not have to criticise anything serious.
rejected.remember: Satire criticises with humour. Parody copies a style to mock it or make a point.

a.q: A writer publishes a mock recipe, with numbered steps and exact amounts, for a school canteen's burnt lunch. What makes it a parody?
opts: Its layout follows the familiar format of a recipe
Its humour pokes fun at the canteen's cooking
Its subject is a lunch that students eat each day
Its claim about the burnt lunch is exaggerated
a.why: A parody imitates the style of another text, and here the writer copies the format of a recipe. Humour and exaggeration aimed at the canteen are tools of satire, so they do not by themselves make a text a parody. The everyday subject has nothing to do with copying a style.
a.clue: A parody needs an original text that readers already know.

b.q: Dev writes a speech in a grand, serious voice. In it, a politician promises to fix traffic by asking every driver to leave home ten minutes earlier. Dev wants readers to see how weak such promises are. Which choice best describes his text?
opts: Satire, as it exaggerates to criticise weak promises
Parody only, as it has no aim beyond copying a style
Satire, as it copies one real speech word for word
Neither, as a serious voice cannot carry any humour
b.why: The silly promise is exaggerated to criticise empty political claims, which is satire. It also copies a grand speech style, so it is a parody as well. The option 'Parody only, as it has no aim beyond copying a style' is tempting because of that copied style, but Dev has a clear target to criticise, which makes it satire.
b.clue: Ask what Dev wants readers to think about politicians.

opts: It copies the style of a recipe to make a point
It gives a serious warning about canteen food

It uses facts to prove the canteen is unsafe
a.why: The writer imitates the recipe format, steps and quantities, so the text is a parody. The other options describe a serious warning, a true account or an argument from facts, and none of these imitates a style.
a.clue: Look at which text form is being copied.
